newsitem.title: UK: UK confident EU will agree Amsterdam treaty.
newsitem.headline: UK confident EU will agree Amsterdam treaty.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government said on Friday it was already making great strides in Europe and predicted it would be able to sign up to a European Union treaty in Amsterdam next month to overhaul the 15-nation bloc.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, speaking after he and Prime Minister Tony Blair met Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, said Britain was being taken seriously once more in Europe now that Labour had drawn a line under the "sterile and negative" attitude of the previous Conservative government.
"I now believe that it will be possible for us to reach an agreement in Amsterdam," Cook told reporters.
"I'm happy to tell you that we're already making substantial progress to getting our objectives," he added.

But Kok, whose government holds the rotating EU presidency, said a number of burning issues still had to be resolved before a new treaty, which he said provided a historic opportunity for Europe, could be wrapped up.
"Without compromises...there will be no treaty of Amsterdam," Kok said.
He said that without the pact, which will redefine some EU powers and streamline its institutions, it would not be possible for the bloc to take in new members from eastern Europe.
"We call upon the political will of all member states to compromise," he said.
Kok said Blair's intention to reverse Conservative policy and sign the EU's social chapter on common workplace standards was an enormous step forward.
"It would really have been impossible to come to further agreement on all the other issues... so this is already something to be very happy about," he said.
But other vital issues had to be resolved, notably whether the EU should have a voice in home affairs and justice and whether member states should work towards a common foreign and security policy.

Other problems were the role of the European parliament, the size of the Brussels-based executive Commission and the question of whether a vanguard of countries should be allowed to forge ahead in certain areas without other member states

"We are very glad that the new British government is of the opinion that they should be a strong and responsible partner in the process of the EU. But we know there are still some problems to be solved on various EU matters between now and Amsterdam," the Dutch prime minister said.
Cook said Britain intended to reach an agreement in Amsterdam provided its national interests were served.
Earlier, a senior government official said Blair would put British interests "first, second and third" in Amsterdam.

One priority for Britain, as an island, is to retain control of immigration. Cook said he and Blair received a positive response from Kok to their demand that Britain be given a clear opt-out from any deal in Amsterdam to give the EU responsibility for external border controls.
The foreign secretary said Kok's visit so soon after Blair took office reflected great European interest in Labour's landslide victory on May 1, which ended 18 years of Conservative rule.

"As a result of that, Mr Blair is in a strong, authoritative position not just in parliament but also in Europe. Britain now negotiates from strength in Westminster and with respect in Europe," he said.
